evidence.claims: Numeric claims in README Results all backed by results.txt and recomputed (checks). Not backed or misleading: (1) README:21-22 frame the cap as 'a price on equivalence proofs ... roughly 93 s each' and Limitations ascribe the kill/proof time gap to 'this solver and design family'; the log shows the gap is set by eda-verify's own phase order and timeouts (BMC first, wall-capped at 210 s, then induction), which the README never mentions (it says only 'Yosys built-in SAT, 22-cycle bound'). (2) 'kills 21 to 164 s' is presented as the separation that makes the cap work, but only 2 formal kills (41 s, 53 s) ever reach formal in any seed; 'no kill lost' rests on two mutants. (3) 'CPU-s' are wall-clock perf_counter seconds of a subprocess (eda-verify checks.py:106-111). Limits and AI-assistance note are present.
evidence.fitness: A researcher can reuse policy.run as a replay tool and the result reproduces in under a second. Building on the headline conclusion would mislead: the obvious alternative policy (run equiv_induct first or cap the BMC phase separately) is not evaluated and, from the log, would keep 15 of 16 proofs for roughly 11-15 s each instead of 93 s. Nearest prior work not cited: mutant-execution timeouts in mutation-analysis cost reduction (Jia and Harman, IEEE TSE 2011 survey), solver runtime prediction and cutoff selection (Hutter et al., Artif. Intell. 2014), and BMC-plus-induction scheduling in formal sign-off flows (e.g. k-induction engines in SymbiYosys/JasperGold). Novelty over those is small; one design, one log, n=2 relevant kills.
evidence.domain: A formal-verification engineer would check the engine script first. eda-verify formal() (research/eda-verify/src/eda_verify/checks.py:117-136) runs 'sat -seq 22 -timeout 150' under a 210 s subprocess wall cap, then equiv_induct under 240 s. In the log (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-oss-monorepo/445518b1-5429-5297-9052-042574ff3b55/scratchpad/aud/phase.py) 16 undecided runs sit at 444.9-450.9 s = 210 + 240, and 15 of 16 equivalence proofs at 221.2-225.2 s = 210 + 11.2..15.2 s: the BMC phase hit its wall cap and induction then proved equivalence in about 12 s. So a single total cap T is really 'skip the induction phase when T < ~221', and the 170 s / 230 s / 93 s-per-proof findings are an artifact of phase ordering, not a property of kill vs proof difficulty. A practitioner would also not call a capped two-phase script's time cap-independent without checking the phases. The replay itself (exact under monotone logged time) is sound.

defects.what: The headline ('a 170 s cap ... gives up all 16 equivalence proofs'; 'the cap is a price on equivalence proofs, roughly 93 s each') is an artifact of eda-verify's formal script, which runs BMC first under a 210 s wall cap and only then equiv_induct. 15 of 16 proofs log at 210 + 11-15 s, so induction alone takes about 12 s; running induction first (or capping phases separately) would keep those proofs for ~180 CPU-s, not ~1,400. The README never states the two-phase structure or the 150/210/240 s timeouts and attributes the gap to 'this solver and design family'.

train_cap (the held-out policy) has no test; three seeded mutations in it or in the undecided branch survive, and test_counts_conserved uses a cap at which no undecided mutant reaches the uncapped branch.

'Kills 21 to 164 s' is presented as the separation the cap exploits, but only two formal kills (41 s, 53 s) ever reach the formal stage and there are zero formal-only kills, so 'no kill lost' for any cap >= 53 s rests on two mutants; the held-out 'learned cap' is trained on one or zero kills.

Nearest prior work (mutant timeouts in mutation-analysis cost reduction, solver cutoff/runtime prediction, BMC/induction engine scheduling) is not cited and the obvious baseline (reorder or per-phase caps) is not evaluated.
Seconds are wall-clock perf_counter around a subprocess, reported as 'CPU-s' / 'CPU time is as logged'.
Imports eda-checkorder by sys.path.insert of a relative sibling path; the dependency is not declared in pyproject.toml, so an installed package fails to import.

When the training half has no formal kill, train_cap returns None and the driver silently substitutes cap 0 (skip formal) rather than the uncapped run; the 'failed' held-out folds are a consequence of that hidden choice.

verdict: Numerically exact and reproducible: run.py regenerates results.txt byte-identical, and three independent re-implementations from the raw eda-verify log match every sweep and held-out row. It does not meet the bar. The interpretation is confounded by the harness: eda-verify's formal stage is BMC (wall-capped at 210 s) followed by induction, and the logged times show 16 undecided runs at 210+240 s and 15 of 16 proofs at 210 + about 12 s, so the '170 s cap loses every proof / proofs cost 93 s each' finding measures the phase order and timeouts, not kill-vs-proof difficulty; a proof-first or per-phase cap would very likely keep the proofs cheaply. Only two formal kills ever reach the capped stage, and 4 of 5 seeded mutations survive the 7 tests (train_cap is untested). Useful as a small replay tool; not something a formal-verification researcher would sign off as a result.
